lawyer:
Mr Miah Abdul Gafur with Mr Mahbubey Alam, Mr. Abbasuddin Ahmed, Mr. Aminuddin, Advocates ------ for the petitioner. 
Mr. Nurul Hoque with Mr. A K M Shahidul Huq, Advocates ------ for the opposite parties.
parties:
Musammat Nurjahan Begum and ors. ------ Petitioners
Vs.
Kamaluddin Ahmed ------ Opposite party
full_judgment:
Syed Amirul Islam, J: This Rule is directed against the judgment and decree dated 15.11.1984 passed by the Subordinate Judge, Narayangonj in Title Appeal No. 185 of 1982 reversing the judgment and decree dated 26.6.1982 passed by the Munsif, 2nd Court, Narayangonj in Title Suit No. 177 of 1979 decreeing the suit.

2. The petitioner as plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 177 of 1979 in the Court of Munsif, Narayangonj for permanent injunction against the defendants restraining them from illegally entering into the suit lands. The plaintiff’s case is that the suit land along with other lands under C.S. Khatian No. 261 of Mouza Fatullah originally belonged to Sonaton Baroi and Ramananda Baroi in equal share. Sonaton Baroi died leaving leaving behind son Shyam Charan Baroi as his heir Ramananda Boroi died leaving 3 daughters. Mohan Mala Biswas, Hari Dasi Baroi and Seba Dasi Baroi as his heirs. By an amicable partition amongst the heirs of Sonaton and Ramananda, the said heirs of Ramananda got the suit plot i.e. C.S. plot No. 393 along with northern half of C.S. plot No. 436 of C.S. khatian No. 261 and they have been in peaceful possession of the suit land and the northern half of the C.S. plot No. 436. The further case of the plaintiff is that the S.A. Khatian of the suit land was wrongly recorded in the name of Shyam Charan which was corrected by compromise decree dated 15.1.75 in Title Suit No. 290 of 1974 of the second Court of Munsif at Narayangonj wherein the right, title, interest and possession of the heirs of Ramananda in the suit plot and the northern half of plot No. 436 was declared and established. While the said Mohan Mala and her two sisters along with their sons were owners in possession of the suit plot along with northern half of the plot No. 436, they enured into a registered agreement dated 4.7.74 to sell the said lands for a consideration of Tk. 25,000/- and received taka 21,000/- as earnest money and delivered possession of the said lands to the plaintiff. Subsequently on 18.2.75 the vendors of the plaintiff executed and registered a saf kabala deed in favour of the plaintiff on receiving the balance consideration of taka 4,000/- from the plaintiff. The plaintiff excavated a tank in the southern portion of the suit land and stacked earth on the northern portion of the suit land for the purpose of manufacturing bricks and has been rearing fishes in the tank. The plaintiff mutated her name in S.A. Khatian in respect of the suit land by mutation case No. 35 FA/75-76 dated 22.7.75 and has been paying rents for the suit land in her name. The name of the plaintiff was duly recorded in the present R.S. Khatian No. 612 of Mouza Fatullah in respect of the suit land. The defendants have/had no right, title, interest and possession over the suit land. The defendants tried to enter into the suit land in the middle part of the month of September, 1979 but could not succeed on account of timely resistance put up by the plaintiff. The defendants gave out that they would enter into the suit land. Hence the plaintiff filed the suit.

3. The defendant opposite parties’ No. 1-3 contested the suit by filing a joint written statement alleging inter-alia that the suit for mere permanent injunction is not at all maintainable as the plaintiff has got no title and possession in the land in question. Their case is that the suit land originally belonged to Sonaton Baroi who died leaving behind his only son Shyam Charan Baroi Shyam Charam Baroi and his son Radha Ballav by a bainapatra dated 20.11.63 agreed to sell the suit property to Mohiuddin father of the defendant No. 1 to 3 and delivered possession of the same to Mohiuddin Ahmed. To enforce the agreement Mohiuddin Ahmed filed Title Suit No. 77 of 1969 for specific performance of contract. The said suit was decreed on 28.1.76 and Kabala was obtained through court on 3.2.78 and got possession of the land in question through court on 11.7.79. The contesting defendant thus contended that they have title and possession in the suit land.

4. The learned Munsif after recording evidence and hearing arguments of both the sides decreed the suit and being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree of the trial court the defendant opposite parties preferred Title Appeal No. 185 of 1982 before the learned District Judge, Narayangonj. The said appeal on transfer was heard by the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Narayangonj on 16.11.1984 and by the impugned judgment and decree he was pleased to set aside the judgment and decree passed by the trial court and dismissed the suit. The plaintiff petitioner being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree of the appellate court below preferred this revisional application and obtained the present Rule.

5. Mr. Miah Abdul Gafur, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff petitioner submits that the judgment of the learned appellate court below is not a proper judgment of reversal because the appellate court below being the final court of fact has not controverts the reasoning and discussion of the trial court inasmuch as the learned appellate court below has not considered and discussed the entire evidence oral and documentary on record and as such this error of law on the part of the appellate court below caused erroneous decision occasioning failure of justice. The learned Advocate further submits that 'the learned appellate court below misread the C.S. khatian No. 261 exhibit 3 C in asmuch as he failed to read the word “গং” after Sonaton Baroi and also failed to read the word “বরাত” in C.S. Khatian No. 76 and the total non-consideration of these material words vitiated the findings of the appellate court below. The learned Advocate further submits that the learned appellate court below erred in law in deciding the question of title of the suit plot in favour of the defendants by wrongly holding that the properties of the disputed C.S. Khatian 76 exhibit 3C belong to Sonaton Baroi, the predecessor of the defendants along although it has been held that the suit is not maintainable for its involvement of complicated question of title. The learned Advocate referring to exhibit 3B and 3C further submits that the learned appellate Court below erred in holding that the learned Munsif is not justified to observe that the land originally belonged to Sonaton Baroi and Ramananda Baroi in equal shares. The learned Advocate with much emphasis submits that the learned appellate court below failed to consider and discuss the various exhibited documents filed by the plaintiff petitioner such as exhibits 1,1A, 2-2A, 3, 3A, 3B, 4A, 5, 6, 6A and also the oral evidence of 5 P.Ws. and those have proved the plaintiff's title and possession in the suit land and as such there is erroneous decision in the matter by the appellate court below occasioning failure of justice. The learned Advocate further submits that exhibit IA, bainapatra and exhibit 3A, S.A. Khatian, exhibit 2-2A rent receipts, exhibit 3 R.S. khatian exhibit 4, 4A containing an admission of Satya Ranjan son of Randha Ballav about the possession and title of the plaintiff petitioner's vendors in the suit plot and evidence of P.Ws. clearly proved the plaintiff's possession and title in the suit land and as such the learned appellate court contrary to those evidence on record erred in dismissing the suit. The learned Advocate finally submits that the defendants could not produce their alleged bainapatra dated 6.11.1963 showing their alleged possession since 1963 and that the defendants case of possession being self contradictory and that D.W.1 and 2 could not give the boundary of the suit plot inasmuch as D.W.1 and 2 are the defendant Nos. 1 and 4 respectively and as such the appellate court below erred in setting aside the decision of the trial court which decreed the suit considering the evidence and materials of the plaintiff vis-a-vis those of the defendants. Mr. Miah Abdul Gafur, the learned Advocate, in support of his contention refers to and relies on the decisions namely (1991)11 BLD (AD)245,37D.L.R.79,PLD1976 (SC)784, 35DLR216 and 6 DLR 271.

6. Mr. Nurul Hoque, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant opposite parties submits that the correct position in that Sonaton Baroi was the sole 16 annas owner of the land of C.S. Khatian No. 261 as will appear on mere reading of the said Khatian exhibit 3C and in a suit for permanent injunction it is of paramount importance that the plaintiff must prove his title to the suit property and unless the plaintiff can show that he has some legal rights and the defendants have legal obligation not to disturb lawful possession of the plaintiff a suit for permanent injunction can not be maintained and in the instant case exhibit 3C clearly shows that the suit land solely belonged to Sonaton Baroi. The learned Advocate further submits that Sonaton Baroi and Ramananda Baroi are sons of two different persons and Ramananda Baroi was not a co-sharer of Sonaton Baroi and as such the question of amicable partition amongst the heirs of Sonaton Baroi and Ramananda Baroi does not arise at all. He further submits that these two persons being stranger to one another the question of any amicable partition between their heirs and such possession on the basis of the said alleged amicable partition does not arise. The learned Advocate further submits that the so called amicable partition if any, was falsely created and the same appears to have been created near about the time when the plaintiff was creating her documents. The learned Advocate further submits that the Title Suit No. 290 of 1974 cannot be a legally tenable suit for correction of S.A. record twelve years after finalization of the said record in 1962 and the trial court failed to take notice of this aspect of the case. Mr. Nurul Huq further submits that the compromise decree was collusive and untenable decree which cannot confer any right, title, interest and possession in favour of the heirs of Ramananda Baroi who was nobody having any interest in the suit land. The learned Advocate further submits that the story of excavation of the tank by the plaintiff is also a cock and bull story which the learned Munsif was hesitant in believing the same reading of the evidences of P.W. 3 and the trial court found major contradiction in evidence along with possession but gave his finding of possession in favour of the plaintiff petitioner without making any comment about the evidence of the D.Ws. which is not a legal decision on assessment of the evidence of both the parties as is called upon to do by the courts of facts and the trial court failed to follow the provisions of the Order 20 Rule 4(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure. Mr. Nurul Huq, the learned Advocate further submits that the mutation in the name of the plaintiff in Mutation Case No. 35/PA/75-76 dated 22.2.75 was not done in a lawful proceeding after service of notices as required under the law. There was no record to show that such mutation was lawfully made, the same was done during pendency of the title suit between the defendants and Satta Ranjan Baroi and as such record is hit by section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act. The recording of the plaintiff's name in the R.S. record was consequential effect of the illegal mutation of the plaintiff's name. In view of the decree obtained by the defendants in Title Suit No. 77 of 1969 the intervening all acts are hit by the doctrine of lis-pendense. The learned Advocate further submits that the trial court misread the C.S. khatian as was rightly found by the learned appellate court below. Mr. Nurul Hoque further submits that the prima facie title of the plaintiff and her possession was not legal finding inasmuch as the khatian No. 261 cannot be construed to show that Sonaton and Ramananda were the joint owner and such contention would be violative of the provisions of section 91 and 92 of the Evidence Act. The learned Advocate finally with much emphasis submits that in the instant case a complicated question of title is involved and the same cannot be decided without evidence in a properly framed suit and in that view of the matter also the learned appellate court below rightly dismissed the suit. Mr. Nurul Hoque, the learned Advocate has referred to and relied on the following decisions namely 1991 BLD (AD) 245, 10 DLR 193. 1982 BCR (AD).

7. Before I enter into the merit of this rule I would like to consider the legal aspect of the case. It appears from the trend of the earlier-judicial pronouncements that in a suit for permanent injunction the plaintiff is to prove exclusive possession of the suit land and incidentally a prima facie title to the suit land. If these two requirements are fulfilled by the plaintiff only the he is entitled to a decree for permanent injunction. If we look to section 110 of the Evidence Act we find that this section embodies the well known principle of Roman law that possession in prima facie proof of ownership and when, therefore, a person is in possession of the property the presumption of ownership is highly in his favour and under section 110 of the Evidence Act the onus of proving that he is not the owner is on the person who affirms that he is not the owner. Similarly section 9 of the Specific Relief Act also protects the possessory right of a person. Title cannot be pleaded in bar in a suit of this nature and the court does not adjudicate upon the title of the parties in a suit under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act. It is thus, clear that even a tress passer can recover his possession if he is dispossessed from immovable property without his consent. If this be so then why a person who is already in possession of an immovable property claiming to be the owner will be required to prove his title to the property in order to protect his possession. In my opinion the correct legal position is that in a suit for permanent injunction the plaintiff need not prove his title to the property as a condition precedent to succeed in an action for permanent injunction It is sufficient if the plaintiff can prove his prior and present possession of the suit land i.e. in a suit for permanent injunction possession is of paramount consideration and the fate of the suit veer round the proof of possession by the plaintiff.

8. From a review of the judicial pronouncements of the Superior Courts of this subcontinent it appears that in order to succeed in a suit for permanent injunction the plaintiff has to prove his exclusive possession and prima facie title. The same trend has undergone a change. Now the superior court emphasize much on the factum of possession and not on the title. It is now well settled that if a man is in continuous possession in the suit he is entitled to protect his right by way of permanent injunction. It has been held in 4BLD127 that a person in long possession can be evicted only in due process of law. Even the rightful owner cannot evict him with force. If he cannot be evicted with force he continues to be in possession and he can resist invasion of his possession by everyone including the rightful owner. If the rightful owner threatened his possession he can pray for an equitable relief of injunction to protect his possession and the remedy of the rightful owner lies in bringing appropriate suit for establishing his right and for recovery of possession.

9. The case reported in 10 DLR 193 was referred to in the said case but it was not followed. In the said 10 DLR case the plaintiff failed to prove his exclusive possession and that was the main ground for refusing the prayer for permanent injunction. Similarly our Appellate Division in the case reported in 4 BLD (AD)285 held that if the plaintiff failed to prove his title in a suit for permanent injunction that will not disentitle him to a decree for permanent injunction if he can prove possession.

10. There are other decisions in that line of both the divisions namely in the case reported in 37 DLR 79 it has been held that law nowhere enjoins that a suit for permanent injunction cannot be maintained without seeking a declaration of title, only because questions of title are raised. As in a partition suit so also in a suit for injunction questions of title may well be raised but that does not mean that without seeking declaration of title a simple suit for partition or a simple suit for injunction cannot be maintained when the plaintiffs are in possession of the land.

11. In the case reported in 11BLD (AD) 245 which has been referred to and relied on by both the sides it has been held that in a simple suit for permanent injunction with regard to a disputed landed property, the relief is available to a person who is in possession. The court may enquire incidentally into the respective claims of the parties to the suit for determining whether the plaintiff has got prima facie case i.e. whether he is in possession of the disputed property and entitled to the specific relief of permanent injunction. In that decision it has been further held that if the dispute involves complicated questions of title, the plaintiff must establish his title by filing a regular suit for declaration of title. 'A simple suit for permanent injunction should not be allowed to be used as a testing device for ascertainment of title.

12. Similarly in the case reported in 1982 BCR (AD) 321 it has been held that in a suit for permanent injunction it is not necessary for the plaintiff to prove his title to the suit property, he is entitled to get a decree of permanent injunction on the basis of his possession.

13. So it is crystal clear that suits for permanent injunction are merely concerned with the factum of possession and not with the nature and character of possession or capacity of the possessor. If the plaintiff is found to be in possession of the suit land he is entitled to get injunction. The principle of Division Bench ruling of the Kerala High Court reported in AIR 1966 (Kerala) 179, also seems to support the view, namely, that a person in possession even if wrongful is entitled to maintain his possession even against true owner, till eviction by due process of law. So the recent judicial pronouncement in this regard is that in a suit for permanent injunction the question of title is of no significance if in a properly framed suit the plaintiff can prove his exclusive possession of the suit land there is no doubt that he is entitled to protect his possession by way of permanent injunction against the whole world including the real owner. In the case reported in PLD 1976(SC) 785 it has been held that it is opened to the plaintiff to frame his suit and couch his relief in any manner within the law. He can sue for relief for declaration of title or permanent injunction or for both or even for declaration and permanent injunction as a consequential relief to suit his own requirement in accordance with law. In that case it has been observed that in this sub-continent declaratory decrees are granted under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act 1972, it lays down that any person is entitled to any legal character, or to any right as to any property. may institute a suit against any person denying his title to such character and the court may in its discretion make therein a declaration that he is so entitled and the plaintiff need not ask for any further relief, provided that no court shall make any such declaration where the plaintiff being able to seek further relief then a declaration of the omits to do so. On the other hand the specific relief by way of perpetual injunction may be granted by the court in accordance with the provisions contained in sections 54 and 56 under Chapter X of the Specific Relief Act. In this connection section 54 inter-alia lays down that a perpetual injunction may be granted to prevent the breach of "obligation" existing in favour of the applicant, whether expressly Of by implication. The term "obligation" is defined in section 3 of the Act as "including every duty enforceable by law" so that when a legal duty is imposed on a person in respect of another, that other is invested with the corresponding legal right. In general under the first paragraph of section 54 of the Act, injunction may be granted by the court to an applicant to prevent the breach of an existing legal right vested in him. It is not always necessary for him to sue for the declaration of his title as a substantive relief and asked for the injunction as a consequential relief only.

14. The case reported in 6 DLR 274 and the other case reported in 35 DLR (AD) 216 has no manner of application in the instant case.

15. Keeping these principles of law in mind let us now scrutinize and examine the impugned judgment and see how far it is sustainable in law. On a perusal of the impugned judgment it appears that the learned appellate court below observed that "It is admitted that to have a relief in the way of permanent in-junction it is the duty of the plaintiff to prove unclouded title and possession in the suit land in default to prove any one of the two will deprive the plaintiff from the cheap relief in the way of permanent injunction. So in a suit for permanent injunction first of all I am to see how far the plaintiff respondent has been able to prove her unclouded title in the land in question which will go to qualify her to have an order of permanent injunction to protect her alleged physical possession in the land in question".

16. From this observation of the learned appellate court below it is crystal clear that the learned appellate court below misdirected himself and treated the instant suit not as a suit for permanent injunction rather treated it as a suit for declaration of title and the said observation is apparently in conflict with the decisions which I have already referred to above. It is, thus, clear that the appellate court below in the instant case travelled beyond the scope of the suit and treating it as a suit for title put much emphasis on the question of title rather than the question of possession.

17. It further appears from the impugned judgment that the learned appellate court below found that the suit plot No. 393 of C.S. khatian No. 261 of mouza Fatullah comprising an area of 1.10 decimals of land originally belonged to Sonaton Baroi alone and this finding of the appellate court below is based on c.s. Khatian No. 261 exhibit 3C in respect of the suit plot No. 393 which speaks that the suit land belonged to Sonaton Baroi alone as a “রায়তী স্থিতিবান”. The learned trial court found that the land recorded in c.s. khatian No. 261 belonged to Sonaton Baroi and Ramananda Baroi in equal shares and the learned appellate court below has reversed that finding observing that in exhibit 3C there is no mentioned that Ramananda Baroi is also 8 annas owner of that jote but this finding of the appellate court below cannot be sustained in law inasmuch as exhibit 3C the c.s. Khatian No. 261 itself shows that Sonaton Baroi and others are the owners and in the column of rent it is written ১৫৯ নং মৌজায় ৭৬ নং খতিয়ানে মোট ৭ ।।৯ পাই Exhibit 3B the c.s. khatian 76 shows that Sonaton Baroi and Ramananda Baroi are the owners of the land recorded in that khatian. Of course, in khatian No. 76 plot No. 83 is recorded whereas the suit plot is recorded in C.S. Khatian No. 261. It is submitted by Mr. Miah Abdul Gafur, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff petitioner, that বরাত mean reference and by referring to the relevant provisions of Technical Rules and Instructions of the Settlement Department, 1957 it has been shown that when tenant have land in different plots in different mouzas the full rent should be entered in one khatian only and cross-reference should be made in all the khatian and as such in the instant case the c.s. Khatian No. 76 and c.s. khatian 261 is to be read together and treated as one document and from this the trial court rightly arrived at a finding that Sonaton Baroi and Ramananda Baroi were equal sharer of the said jote. He has referred to the definition of "jote" as contained in section 5 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. "Jote' does not necessarily mean the interest of a cultivator, or an occupancy holding; it is only a general term and may mean a raiyati, under raiyati or any sort of holding for the purpose of cultivation. It simply connotes a tenancy. So if exhibit 3B and 3C are considered together it appears that the finding of the trial court is at least correct with regard to the prima facie title of the predecessor in interest46of the plaintiff petitioner in the suit land and the observation of the learned appellate court below cannot be maintained in view of the fact that in arriving at such a finding that Sonaton Baroi is the sole owner of the c.s. Khatian No. 393 is based on misreading of exhibit 3B as well as 3C because in exhibit 3C itself in column of owner it is written "owner is Sonaton Baroi and others and in the column of rent it is written “১৫৯ নং মৌজায় ৭৬ নং খতিয়ানে মোট ৭ ।।৯ পাই ” and the learned appellate court has failed to take notice of the contents of exhibit 3C and 3B and totally misread exhibit 3C and therefore the finding of the learned appellate Court below that Sonaton Baroi is the Sole owner of the suit land is absolutely contrary to the materials and evidence on record. At least there is prima facie evidence to show that both Sonatan Baroi and Ramananda were 8 annas share of the land recorded in 2 Khatians namely C. S. Khatian No. 261 and 76. On top of that the R.S. Khatian also stand in the name of the plaintiff petitioner. It is submitted that this R.S. Khatian has been published in the year 1974 in the district of Narayanganj by virtue of section 144 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. This RS. Khatian also has a presumptive value and this R.S. Khatian has been published after conducting field survey. In that view of the matter also it can be said that the plaintiff petitioner has been able to prove his prima facie title and possession in the suit land. If these 3 documents are considered along with the oral evidence of all the P.Ws. and D.Ws. it appears that the finding of the trial court that the plaintiff has been able to prove her prima facie title and exclusive possession in the suit land cannot be assailed. I, thus, find that the finding of the appellate court below that C.S. plot No. 393 entirely belonged to Sonatan Baroi is erroneous and contrary to the materials and evidence on record.

18. It further appears from the impugned judgment that the learned appellate court below did not give his finding on all the documents on the ground that in a simple suit for permanent injunction all those things need not be discussed and in that view of the matter he did not give has definite finding on exhibit 4, 4A and other documents filed by the plaintiff petitioner in support of her title and the learned appellate court below has rightly refrained himself from making any positive finding as to the legality and validity of these documents as in the instant suit the court is not called upon to adjudicate on the title rather the court is to see as to whether the plaintiff petitioner is in possession of the suit land and whether she is entitled to protect her possession by way of permanent injunction. The learned appellate court below arrived at a finding that the instant suit involves a complicated question of title and it cannot be decided in a suit for permanent injunction. It is true that in a suit for permanent injunction title cannot be gone into and it cannot be adjudicated upon but if it is found that the suit as framed comes within the ambit of section 54 of the Specific Relief Act the plaintiff is entitled to get a decree of permanent injunction inasmuch as in a suit for permanent injunction the question of title is of no significance at all.

19. It also appears on a perusal of the impugned judgment that although the learned appellate court below refrained himself from giving any positive finding on the question of title of the parties to the suit land, nevertheless, it has observed that the findings and decisions of the trial court in respect of the title of the suit land is erroneous and as such the learned appellate court below held that the suit is not maintainable but this finding of the appellate court below cannot be sustained in law in as much as in a suit for permanent injunction the fate of the suit cannot depend on the question of title of the plaintiff. The finding of the learned appellate court below that the acquisition of title of the plaintiff petitioner through heir of Ramananda Baroi cannot be considered to be good and no relief can be given to the plaintiff petitioner in the instant suit for permanent injunction is unwarranted and uncalled for in asmuch as in arriving at such a finding the learned appellate court below travelled beyond the scope of the suit.

20. Regarding physical possession of the suit land the appellate court below relying on the deposition of two D.Ws. and writ issued in pursuance of the Title Execution Case No. 19 of 1976 has arrived at a finding that at least the defendants have been able to prove symbolical possession in the suit land after successful termination of the Title Suit No. 77 of 1969 in their favour but in arriving at such a finding the appellate court below lost sight of the two c.s. khatians being khatian No.76 and khatian No. 261 and the R.S. khatian exhibit 3 and rent receipts exhibit 2-2A and the oral evidence of P.Ws. which conclusively proved the possession of the plaintiff petitioner in the suit land. It thus appears that the finding of the learned appellate court below that the defendants have been able to prove at least their symbolical possession of the suit land does not inspire confidence and the finding of the trial court on that point is backed by sufficient materials and evidence on record both oral and documentary.

21. It appears on a perusal of the impugned judgment that the learned appellate court below misdirected himself and treated the instant suit as a suit for declaration of title and confirmation of possession in asmuch as he has observed that the plaintiff petitioner has failed to prove her unclouded title and possession in the suit land. It thus appears to me that the learned appellate court below absolutely misappreciated the scope of the suit and travelled beyond the scope of the instant suit and arrived at such finding which is contrary to the established principles of law and in that view of the matter also the findings arrived at by the appellate court below at least on possession cannot be sustained.

<u>22. One of the grievances of Mr. Miah Abdul Gafur is that the impugned judgment is not a proper judgment of reversal. The learned Advocate for the plaintiff petitioner has argued that the impugned judgment passed by the appellate court below is not a proper judgment of reversal in as much as the object of the Rule 31 of Order 41 of the Code of Civil Procedure has not been complied with by the appellate court below. This contention of the learned Advocate for the plaintiff petitioner appears to be well founded. The object of Rule 31 of Order 41 of the Code is to see that a Judge does not act callously or even mechanically. Its purpose is to put the Judge on the right track and to the extent Rule of Procedure can do it, to see that he acts judicially. It enables the High Court to Judge whether the appellate court below had independently considered the case with a consciousness of relevant points which arose for adjudication. It is also to afford the parties opportunity of knowing the grounds of decision to enable them to exercise the right of revision and to enable the High Court Division in revision to see whether lower appellate court has properly appreciated and decided the case. Appellate judgment reversing the judgment of trial court should be adequate and satisfactory. It must contain definite findings on the questions involved and must give reasons for reversing the decisions of the trial court. In fact judgment of reversal may often need a little more discussion of facts, evidence and points involved in the case so as to embody in it convincing reasons for reversing the findings of the courts of first instance. It should cover almost entire grounds covered by the judgment appealed from. It must express opinion on all points on which the lower court has based its conclusion. It is not necessary for lower appellate court to mention each and every particular item of evidence in its judgment provided it is clear upon reading of the judgment itself that all relevant evidence has been substantially considered by the appellate court below. The appellate judgment may not meet all reasons given in the judgment of the trial court while setting it aside. The appellate court must advert to the findings and reasoning’s assigned by the trial court. These principles had not been followed by the appellate court below in as much as in some places appellate court grossly misread the evidence and the impugned judgment suffers from non-reading and non-consideration of the materials and evidence on record. The trial court discussed the evidence on the point of possession with regard to both oral and documentary evidence and after close scrutiny of the same have relied on the testimonies of the P.Ws. and discarded the testimonies of the D.Ws. on that point. The appellate court below failed to consider the assertions made by the parties in respect of possession of the suit property and also failed to notice the fact that in the instant case the defendants have failed to produce the agreement by virtue of which they have filed Title Suit No. 77 of 1969 and got an exparte decree and they have not been able to prove the said agreement even in the instant case. The learned appellate court below also failed to take notice of the fact that the case of possession is self contradictory inasmuch as in the said suit for specific performance of contract the defendant opposite parties have asserted that they have entered into possession of the suit land in 1963 in pursuance of bainapatra whereas in his evidence the D.W. 1 who is the defendant No. 1 asserted that they entered into possession of the suit land, through the court after execution of the decree of Title Suit No. 77 of 1974. The trial court dealt with the matter in detail but the learned appellate court below did not advert to it in its judgment. In 14 BLD (AD)229 it has been held by their Lordship that the appellate court whether reversing or affirming the decision of the trial court must independently consider the evidence on record but in the case of affirming the findings of the trial court, the narration of the entire evidence and reiteration of the reasons given by the trial court are not essential. In such a case expressions of general agreement with those of the trial court are generally considered sufficient. But in the case of reversal of the judgment the consideration of the evidence, of necessity, has to be thoroughly and more elaborate. But in the instant case it is crystal clear from the impugned judgment that the learned appellate court below failed to advert to the evidences both oral and documentary adduced by the plaintiff petitioner and the learned appellate court below also failed to reverse the finding of the trial court by giving cogent reason therefor. It has been held in the case reported in 15 BLD (AD) 120 that while exercising revisional power under section 115 of the Civil Procedure Code the High Court usually does not go into the question of fact but when the appellate court reverse the judgment of the trial court on non consideration of the materials on record and without adverting to the reasoning on which the trial court gave its judgment, the High Court may be justified to interfere with the findings of fact arrived at by the appellate court when it finds that non-consideration of such evidence has materially affected the appellate court judgment occasioning failure of justice. In the light of the aforesaid principles of law also the impugned judgment cannot be sustained in law.</u>

23. It has been argued by Mr. Nurul Hoque, the learned Advocate for the defendant opposite parties that in a suit for permanent injunction a party cannot be prevented by an order of injunction when in exercise of his legal rights to the suit land he wants to enter into possession because in section 3 of the Specific Relief Act "obligation" includes every duty enforceable by law and section 5B of the said Act provides that specific relief can be given by ordering a party to do very act which he is under an obligation to do. Section 5C provides that the specific relief can be given by preventing a party from doing that which he is under an obligation not to do and section 54 of the S.R. Act runs as follows:-

"Subject to the other provisions contained in, or referred by this Chapter a perpetual injunction may be granted to prevent the breach of an obligation existing in favour of the applicant, whether expressly or by implication. "When such obligation arises from contract, the court shall be guided by the rules and provisions contained in"Chapter 2 of the Act".

It thus appears that in a suit for permanent injunction the plaintiff is entitled to get an order in his favour only when the plaintiff can prove that the defendant is under an obligation either not to do an act which is threatened by him or to do an act which he refuses to do. In other words the defendants must be under a legal obligation either to do an act and not to do an act. He further submits that in that view of the matter if it is a contesting claim of title in a disputed property the plaintiff cannot resist the defendant from disturbing him with his possession of the defendant can show that he has legal right to the suit land. This argument is very much convincing but I cannot accept the same in view of the decisions of our Appellate Division as has already been referred to above. In the light of the aforesaid decisions it appears to me that in a suit for permanent injunction if the plaintiff can show his exclusive possession of the suit land, even independently of his title, he is entitled to get an order of injunction against the defendant.

<u>24. From my aforesaid discussion it is crystal clear that in a suit for permanent in-junction there is no scope to adjudicate upon the question of title of the parties although the court can incidentally can go to the question of title. In that view of the matter the court should be conscious in making any observation touching the merit of title of either parties. On a scrutiny of the trial court's judgment it appears that the trial court has made certain observations which are actually relevant in determining the question of title. It has already been found that title is of no significance in a suit for permanent injunction and as such the observation made by the trial court regarding title of the parties are unwarranted, uncalled for and must be expunged. So, the finding of the trial court that "It gives a strong presumption that they merely created a document of title to and possession over the suit land by filing the aforesaid execution case for delivery of possession" and the finding of the trial court that "On perusal of the documents it appears that as per C.S. Khatian both Sonaton and Ramananda are equal shares (8 annas each) in the land of suit khatian" are expunged.</u>

25. In this connection it may be stated that the observation of the trial court with regard exhibit 4, 4A, 5, 3, 3A, 2-2A, 1 and 1A that is all the documents exhibited by the plaintiff before the trial court should not be treated as a positive finding as to the genuinely or otherwise of the aforesaid deeds as in a suit for permanent injunction the court need not and should not enter into the question of title. The observations of the trial court with regard to the aforesaid documents are merely incidental and neither of the courts below had any jurisdiction at all to adjudicate upon the legality or validity of these documents in the instant suit. The validity and legality of these documents will be determined in a properly framed suit and these observations of the trial court will not stand on the way of either party in future in a properly framed suit and in that view of the matter the validity and legality of these documents are kept open to be adjudicated upon in future in an appropriate suit.

26. In view of my aforesaid discussion I find substance in this revisional application. In the result the Rule is made absolute. The judgment and decree dated 15.11.84 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Narayangonj in Title Appeal No. 185 of 1982 are set aside and the judgment and decree dated 26.6.1982 passed by the learned Munsif, 2nd Court, Narayangonj in Title Suit No. 177 of 1979 are restored.

27. In view of the facts and circumstances of the case there will be no order as to cost.

End.
